passage:
Elif had not spoken to Layla since Tuesday, and it was now Thursday night in their Toronto dorm room. She moved around Layla like furniture: headphones in, back turned, lamp clicked off at ten without the usual "night".
Layla lay awake replaying the week. Was it the seat she forgot to save at the lecture? The charger she returned late? The mug left in the sink? She wrote three apology texts, each longer than the last, and sent them all. "I'm so sorry for everything, whatever it was."
Read. No reply.
Her chest ached in a way that felt almost physical. She skipped the study group on Friday in case Elif wanted to talk. Elif didn't.
When Layla's sister called, she said she was fine. Then she hung up and realised she had apologised four times in a call about nothing.

qa.q: What did Layla send after lying awake?
qa.a: She sent three apology texts, each longer than the last.

qa.q: What was Layla feeling as she replayed the week?
qa.a: She felt dread and an almost physical ache in her chest, desperate to find what she had done so the silence would end.

qa.q: What could Layla do instead of apologising for everything?
qa.a: She could say once, calmly, that she will talk when Elif is ready, keep going to the study group, and tell her sister honestly how the silence is affecting her.

qa.q: What would change if Elif had said "I'm upset about the seat, give me a day"?
qa.a: Layla would know what was wrong and that the silence would end, so she could apologise for the real thing and sleep instead of replaying everything.

grounding: A student frozen out by Elif spends days replaying the week and apologising for anything, feeling the silence as real pain.

passage:
Rashmi had typed and deleted the same message nine times on the office computer. "Rajni ma'am, sorry if I overstepped yesterday."
Yesterday, in the newsroom meeting, she had pointed out a spelling mistake in a headline Rajni had written. Since then Rajni had walked past her desk three times without a glance, handed out the day's stories to every intern except her, and laughed with the others by the water cooler.
Rashmi's stomach knotted every time the glass door swung. She reread her notes from the meeting. Had she sounded rude? By lunch she had apologised to the photo editor for borrowing a stapler and to the office assistant for being in the way.
At four she walked to Rajni's desk. "I'm really sorry about yesterday. It won't happen again."
Rajni didn't look up. "Hm."
Rashmi went back to her chair feeling smaller than when she had started.

qa.q: What mistake did Rashmi point out in the meeting?
qa.a: She pointed out a spelling mistake in a headline Rajni had written.

qa.q: Why did Rashmi's stomach knot every time the glass door swung?
qa.a: She felt dread about Rajni's coldness and was on edge, bracing for more rejection.

qa.q: What could Rashmi do instead of apologising for a correct correction?
qa.a: She could remind herself that spotting a real mistake was not wrong, ask someone senior she trusts how to handle being left out, and get her stories assigned through the proper channel.

qa.q: What would change if Rajni had simply said "Thanks, fixed it"?
qa.a: Rashmi would feel her care for detail was valued, and she would not spend the day apologising to everyone for small things.

grounding: An intern ignored by Rajni after correcting a headline replays the moment, apologises for anything and ends the day feeling smaller.

passage:
I'm Harsha, and I still remember the week Devika stopped talking to me.
It was a Monday. I'd joked about her new haircut in the canteen, lightly, I thought. She smiled. Then, that night, nothing. My messages sat unread. The next day in class, she looked straight through me.
I couldn't eat. I lay awake replaying every word. Was it the haircut joke? Was it something from last week? I apologised for the joke. Then for being late on Friday. Then for something I said in October. I sent six messages. She didn't answer any.
By Thursday I was apologising for things I didn't even think were wrong. I just wanted the silence to end. Every hour of it felt like being shut out of a room I needed.
On Saturday she replied, "I'm fine." Nothing else. I cried with relief. I was that frightened of being ignored.

qa.q: How many messages did Harsha send?
qa.a: Harsha sent six messages.

qa.q: How did Harsha feel during the week of silence?
qa.a: Harsha felt dread and anxiety, unable to eat or sleep, desperate for the silence to end.

qa.q: What could help Harsha next time someone goes silent?
qa.a: Harsha could ask once, calmly, what happened, then talk to a trusted friend instead of apologising for everything.

qa.q: How might Devika have seen the week?
qa.a: Devika may have felt angry or hurt about the joke, but her silence gave Harsha no chance to understand or repair it.

grounding: A young adult recalls dread and frantic apologies under a friend's sudden silence, showing how ignoring causes real social pain.

passage:
Hostel warden's note, boys' hostel, Wednesday.
Eshaan came to my office this evening, pale. He said his girlfriend, Mahima, has not spoken to him for four days after an argument about his exam schedule. She reads his messages but doesn't reply.
He showed me his phone. Twenty-three messages. Most of them were apologies: for the argument, for not calling on Sunday, for "being too much," for things he couldn't even name. He hasn't slept properly. He missed a test on Tuesday.
He kept asking me, "What did I do?" I told him that being ignored like this causes real pain, and that his reaction is normal, not weak.
We talked about sending one calm message saying he's willing to talk when she's ready, and then stopping. I've booked him with the student counsellor tomorrow at ten, and asked his roommate to check on him tonight.

qa.q: How many messages had Eshaan sent?
qa.a: Twenty-three messages.

qa.q: How was Eshaan feeling when he came to the warden?
qa.a: Eshaan felt anxious and frightened, pale and sleepless, apologising for anything because of the silence.

qa.q: What steps did the warden take to help?
qa.a: The warden reassured him his pain was normal, suggested one calm message, booked the counsellor for the next day and asked his roommate to check on him.

qa.q: How might Mahima's silence look from Eshaan's side?
qa.a: From Eshaan's side, it feels frightening and endless, making him replay everything and apologise even for things he can't name.

grounding: A warden notes a young adult frightened and over-apologising under a partner's four-day silence, and responds with care.

passage:
Sunday night
Pema still isn't talking to me. Day three.
It started on Thursday. I said I couldn't come to the concert because of my shift. Pema said "fine." Then, silence. Not angry words. Just nothing. Unread messages. When I went to the flat, Pema's flatmate said Pema was "busy."
I've replayed Thursday a hundred times. Was it my tone? Should I have swapped the shift? I've apologised four times. I apologised for the shift, for my tone, for last month's thing, for "everything."
My stomach hurts all the time. I keep checking my phone in the bathroom at work.
I know this isn't fair. I didn't do anything cruel. I had a shift. But being ignored makes me feel like I'm disappearing.
Tomorrow I'm calling my sister. I need someone to tell me I'm not crazy.
Ojas

qa.q: Why couldn't Ojas come to the concert?
qa.a: Because of the shift.

qa.q: How has Ojas been feeling during the silence?
qa.a: Ojas feels anxious and hurt, with a constant stomach ache, and like disappearing while being ignored.

qa.q: What small step does Ojas plan for tomorrow?
qa.a: Ojas plans to call a sister to get an outside view instead of apologising again.

qa.q: How might Pema's flatmate see the situation?
qa.a: The flatmate may feel awkward being in the middle, saying Pema is busy without explaining.

grounding: A diary shows a young adult full of dread and repeated apologies during a partner's silence, feeling the real pain of being ignored.

Monday 9:12 pm, Binita: hey, you ok? you went quiet after dinner
Monday 11:40 pm, Binita: was it what I said about your cousin? I didn't mean it badly
Tuesday 7:05 am, Binita: I'm really sorry for whatever I did
Tuesday 1:30 pm, Binita: Santosh please just say something
(Seen. No reply.)
Tuesday 1:34 pm, Binita to Mala: he's not talking to me again. 2 days. I can't eat
Mala: what happened?
Binita: I don't even know. I keep replaying dinner. maybe it was the cousin thing. or I laughed too loud
Mala: did you do something wrong, or does he just go silent when he's annoyed?
Binita: ...the second one. every time. and I always end up saying sorry for things I can't name
Mala: that sounds exhausting. come to mine after class, we'll eat together, and you can decide calmly what you want to say, if anything

qa.q: How long had Santosh not been talking to Binita?
qa.a: Two days.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling as the messages went unanswered?
qa.a: Binita felt dread and anxious guilt, replaying dinner, unable to eat, and apologising for something Binita couldn't even name.

qa.q: How does Mala help?
qa.a: Mala asks whether Binita did anything wrong or whether this is a pattern, says it sounds exhausting, and offers food and calm time to decide.

qa.q: How does Mala seem to see Santosh's silence?
qa.a: Mala seems to see it as a habit that leaves Binita apologising for unnamed things, not as proof that Binita did wrong.

grounding: Shows a young adult under a partner's silence who feels dread, replays everything and rushes to apologise for things they cannot name.
